name: Lena Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, which has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does a usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the steel bracket press at a factory making parts for household appliances. I have a two-year technical diploma and know the dies well enough to hear when one starts leaving a burr. My pay is above the usual operator rate, and I teach a young apprentice to check the guard before a run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the plant, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My fiancé Mateo is a carpenter, and we have no children yet; we are saving for a home near our families. More than six months of costs are already set aside, and plenty of metal factories are nearby. I have never used an AI tool and prefer to read the press and the first part myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stamping crew that the office can tidy its reports, but we still need a clean die and two hands outside the guard. I do not use AI and have no reason to start on this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bracket orders are regular and I am paid well to lead the press setup. My fiancé Mateo and I have more than six months saved, and other metal factories nearby could take an experienced operator if this one slowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the dies and gauging the first bracket of each run. In the first year of a plateau I would put a fresh part of each wage into our house deposit account, then teach the apprentice the manual stop routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and glad to get on with the job. I would rather spend lunch talking about the wedding than another screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the apprentice check before a press run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She checks that the guard latches, then keeps her hands clear while I jog the press slowly. A bracket with a raised burr goes back through inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the deposit already saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already have a good cushion, but this would be extra money from each new wage. Mateo and I are not calling the same cash a new deposit twice.

say: I would tell the **stamping crew** a clean die and guard matter more than an office report.
I would keep **AI tools** off my own press routine.
think: Regular **bracket orders** and higher pay make my job feel secure.
Our **savings** and nearby factories give Mateo and me options.
do: Set the **press dies** and gauge the first bracket each run.
Transfer **fresh wage money** to our house deposit monthly.
Teach the **apprentice** the guard and stop routine.
feel: **Calm**, with attention on the press and our wedding plans.
S0.quote: A bracket with a raised burr goes back through inspection.
fieldNote: Lena has **never used AI** and puts her trust in physical guard and gauge checks.
The deposit transfer is **new saving from wages**, while strong pay and nearby jobs support calm.

steps.text: Keep setting press dies and checking first brackets
Add new wages to the house deposit each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management that quicker ordering is fine if the apprentices still get a paid shift beside the press. Office planning changes first, but a hurried press setup can injure someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead job ought to stay for now, and Mateo’s carpentry bookings are steady. I worry that they may stop hiring apprentices, yet our two incomes and savings are not under a direct threat in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the production manager for the next apprentice rota and keep leading the morning setups. If a new screen reaches the press, I would ask for an in-person paid demonstration, then decide whether it is part of the safe method before touching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the young workers. I am not losing sleep over my own wage, but a factory with nobody learning has a short future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which apprentice shift would you protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first full setup shift after a die change. An apprentice needs to see a real jam cleared safely, not just a video of an easy run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sign up for AI training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used an AI tool, and nobody has offered a press control course. I would ask to see the actual screen first, with paid time.

say: I would ask management to keep **paid apprentice shifts** during faster office scheduling.
I would insist on a **safe setup** before any speed target reaches the press.
think: My **lead pay** and Mateo’s carpentry work look steady for now.
A missing **apprentice intake** would weaken the trade even if I stay employed.
do: Request the **apprentice rota** from the production manager.
Keep the **morning press setups** and guard checks.
Request an **in-person paid demonstration** only if a new screen reaches my station.
feel: **Uneasy** for apprentices while our own household wages remain steady.
S1.quote: An apprentice needs to see a real jam cleared safely, not just a video of an easy run.
fieldNote: Her concern stays with the **apprentice route**, consistent with secure household income.
She requests a **demonstration**, not an assumed course or actual use of new controls.

steps.text: Keep morning press setups and guard checks
Request an in-person paid demonstration if a new press screen arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI may change office plans by 2028, when I am twenty nine, but capable stamping robots come around 2031. A press robot needs a proved guard and a human stop before anyone calls it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At thirty two the physical press work could shrink, and I cannot assume they will keep the lead operator. Mateo’s carpentry income may also be affected later, though our savings and local factories buy us search time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep our planned wedding small and postpone the house purchase until we see actual press orders. If two rosters remove my lead hours, I would apply to a posted nearby press job only at a comparable rate and with a written safe setup role; I would keep earning here meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the hours and about starting married life on a guess. Our house deposit is useful, but it will not replace two wages forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate a robot in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request to watch a paid supervised run behind the guard. I would touch the controls only if offered paid instruction and a safety lead has tested the stop; no such place is promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move in with family if the press wage fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo and I would first use the cushion and look at real local openings. We would ask my parents about a short stay only if both wages fell and the rent became hard to cover.

say: I would separate **2028 office AI** from capable stamping robots around 2031.
I would demand a **guarded supervised trial** before a robot enters the press area.
think: My **lead hours** may shrink in 2031, with Mateo’s income uncertain too.
Savings and **nearby factories** provide options without promising the same wage.
do: Postpone the **house purchase** until press orders and our wages are clearer.
Apply after **two reduced rosters** to a posted comparable-pay safe press role.
Keep **current shifts** while they remain paid and safe.
feel: **Anxious** about two wages and a house plan during a fast change.
S2.quote: Our house deposit is useful, but it will not replace two wages forever.
fieldNote: She watches for a **two-roster trigger** before applying to a real local vacancy.
Her robot involvement stays a **request to observe**, with hands-on controls conditional on paid safe instruction.

steps.text: Postpone house purchase until press orders and wages are clearer
Apply after two reduced rosters to posted nearby comparable-pay press role with written safe setup
Keep current shifts while paid and safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew we have until 2031 for thinking AI and roughly 2034 before capable robots run hands-on stamping. That is time to teach a safe die change instead of rushing everyone through a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty two when plans change and thirty five when the press itself is at risk. A few years of good wages could strengthen the deposit, but I still do not want to train for a role that has no posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the current line and put a new amount from each wage toward the house. If the company offers a fully funded practical maintenance course on paid time, with a posted nearby role at comparable pay, I would enrol and then apply after qualifying; otherwise I would keep my press job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though I can see a route if it is real. I will learn a bearing repair with a fitter, not pretend a video makes me a mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical training have to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate the press and let me replace a worn bearing on a stopped unit. The course needs an offered workshop place and paid study hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course without a job posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A certificate without a comparable-pay vacancy is too much risk, even with savings. I would rather stay on the press and watch actual openings.

say: I would ask for **safe die teaching** during the years before physical robots.
I would distinguish **2031 planning AI** from 2034 hands-on change.
think: Good **current wages** can strengthen our deposit before robots arrive.
A **maintenance certificate** only helps if a real comparable-pay job is posted.
do: Keep the **current press line** and add new wages to the house account.
Enrol in **funded paid-time maintenance training** only with an offered workshop place and posted comparable-pay role.
Apply after **qualifying** for that local safe maintenance job.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a path only if training and vacancy conditions are real.
S3.quote: I will learn a bearing repair with a fitter, not pretend a video makes me a mechanic.
fieldNote: Her first preference remains **familiar press work**, despite accepting a practical paid course if needed.
The enrolment and later **job application** each depend on an offered workshop place, funding, paid time and a posted fair-wage role.

steps.text: Keep current press line and add fresh wages to house account
Enrol in funded paid-time maintenance course if workshop place and posted equal-pay job exist
Apply after qualifying for posted local equal-pay maintenance job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office has ten years until thinking AI in 2036, while capable press robots come around 2039. The extra three years for the physical line should be used for real apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty seven at the thinking date and forty when capable press robots arrive. Mateo and I may have a house and children by then, so wages still matter even with savings; nobody can promise a lifetime press post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, in 2026, I would keep supervising die changes and add fresh wages to the house account. In the first year after 2036 I would check the actual press roster and nearby postings; if still on a paid safe line I would work it, but after a sustained lead-hour cut I would apply only for a posted comparable-pay safe role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant pay risk, but settled enough to plan. A press apprentice needs a real shift before anyone says the future is already decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What apprenticeship change would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant manager to keep paid die-change practice on the roster, with a qualified operator beside each apprentice. It has to be a real shift, not an after-hours favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a speculative course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use my technical diploma and current job while they pay. I would consider a practical funded course with paid time and a posted local vacancy if the need becomes real.

say: I would call for **paid apprenticeships** before 2039 press robots arrive.
I would keep **2036 office change** distinct from later physical automation.
think: At **forty**, I may need a wage for a house and children.
Our **savings** cushion change without guaranteeing a lifetime press job.
do: Keep **die-change supervision** now and put new wages into the house account.
Check **2036 rosters and postings** before applying after a sustained lead-hour cut.
feel: **Uneasy** about later income, with time to plan for family needs.
S4.quote: A press apprentice needs a real shift before anyone says the future is already decided.
fieldNote: Lena uses the long horizon for **current paid work** and a practical apprentice request.
Her post-2036 employment is **conditional** on safe paid shifts or an actual comparable-pay local vacancy after cuts.

steps.text: Keep supervising die changes while adding new wages to house account
Apply after sustained lead-hour cuts to posted comparable-pay safe local role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a robot could cut my lead hours by 2031 while Mateo and I are planning a home. A guarded paid demonstration and posted nearby press jobs at a comparable rate would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the apprentice when a manager stops paying for real setup shifts. A factory cannot inherit the sound of a worn die from a screen.

headlineQuote: A factory cannot inherit the sound of a worn die from a screen.
portrait: **Lena**, 27, leads an appliance bracket press with a two-year technical diploma and above-usual operator pay.
She and fiancé **Mateo** have substantial savings, no children yet and many nearby factories as possible alternatives.
She has **never used AI**, prefers familiar press methods and requires guarded proof before learning unfamiliar controls.
Her **house plan** makes potential lead-hour cuts matter, while she presses for paid apprentice practice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to lost press hours by 2031 during Lena’s planned house purchase.
whatWouldHelp: A **guarded paid demonstration** and posted comparable-pay local press roles would help her decide.
